column9: A free-body diagram (FBD) is a drawing of an object that shows –
column14: the path the object travels and how far it goes
column15: every force the object exerts on the objects around it
column16: the object's speed and the time it takes to move
column17: only the forces acting on the object, with their relative size and direction
column28: An FBD includes only the forces acting on the object and shows the relative size (arrow length) and direction of each force. It does not show forces the object exerts on other things, and it is not a map of the object's path.
column29: FBDs are about forces only. Which choice talks about the size and direction of forces on the object?

column9: Match each FBD label to the force it stands for.
column15: FN :: Normal force
column16: Fapp :: Applied force
column17: Ff :: Friction
column28: Fg = force of gravity (weight), FN = normal force, Fapp = applied force, Ff = friction, Fair = air resistance, T = tension (a string, rope, or cable).
column29: Look at the letters after the F: g for gravity, N for normal, app for applied, f for friction.

column9: Saffron's science book sits at rest on her desk. On an FBD, which way does the normal force (FN) on the book point?
column15: Straight up
column16: To the right
column17: There is no normal force on a book at rest
column28: The normal force is perpendicular to the surface and keeps the book on top of the desk, so on a level desk it points straight up. Gravity (Fg) is the arrow that points down.
column29: The normal force keeps objects from falling through the surface they sit on.

column9: On an FBD, the friction arrow points in the same direction the object is moving.
column28: False. Friction opposes motion, so it always points opposite the direction of motion. A box slid to the right has its Ff arrow pointing left.
column29: Does friction help the motion or work against it?

column9: Forces that are equal in size and opposite in direction, so they cancel out, are called ___ forces.
column28: Balanced forces are equal and opposite, so the net force is 0 N and the motion does not change. Unbalanced forces produce a net force.
column29: Think of a tug-of-war where neither team moves.

column9: Jae pushes a cart with 25 N to the right while Addy pulls the same cart with 15 N to the right. The net force on the cart is ___ N to the right. What number goes in the blank? Answer in N.
column28: Forces in the same direction add. Formula: Fnet = F1 + F2. Set up: Fnet = 25 N + 15 N. Answer: 40 N to the right.
column29: Both forces point the same way. Do you add or subtract?

column9: A box has a 30 N force pushing it to the left and a 12 N force pushing it to the right. The net force is ___ N to the left. What number goes in the blank? Answer in N.
column28: Forces in opposite directions subtract, and the net force points toward the bigger force. Formula: Fnet = Fbig − Fsmall. Set up: Fnet = 30 N − 12 N. Answer: 18 N to the left. (Adding to get 42 N is the common mistake.)
column29: The forces point opposite ways. Subtract the smaller from the larger.

column9: Wyatt is skydiving straight down. Which way does the air resistance (Fair) arrow point on his FBD?
column14: Down, the same way he falls
column15: Toward the airplane he jumped from
column16: Up, opposite the way he falls
column17: There is no arrow because air has no mass
column28: Air resistance acts opposite the direction of motion. Wyatt is falling down, so Fair points up. Gravity (Fg) is the arrow pointing down.
column29: Air resistance works against the motion. Which way is Wyatt moving?

column9: A pumpkin sitting still on a porch has no forces acting on it.
column28: False. Gravity (Fg) pulls the pumpkin down and the porch pushes up with the normal force (FN). The forces are balanced, so the net force is 0 N, but the forces are still there.
column29: Is gravity still pulling on the pumpkin? What stops it from falling through the porch?

column9: Storm pushes a dresser across the carpet to the right at a constant speed. How do the applied force (Fapp) and friction (Ff) arrows compare on the FBD?
column15: Ff is longer than Fapp
column16: Fapp is drawn but Ff is left off
column17: Fapp and Ff are the same length
column28: Constant speed means the forces are balanced (Type A), so the Fapp and Ff arrows are the same length and point in opposite directions. A longer Fapp would make the dresser speed up.
column29: Constant speed means no change in motion. What does that tell you about the net force?

column9: A sign hangs at rest from one rope. Which forces belong on the sign's FBD?
column15: FN up and Fg down
column16: T up, FN up, and Fg down
column17: Fg down only
column28: The rope pulls up on the sign (tension, T) and gravity pulls down (Fg). The sign is at rest, so the two arrows are the same length. There is no normal force because the sign is not sitting on a surface.
column29: What holds the sign up? What pulls it down?

column9: In tug-of-war, the blue team pulls the rope left with 200 N and the gold team pulls it right with 200 N. What is the net force on the rope? Answer in N.
column28: Equal forces in opposite directions are balanced. Set up: Fnet = 200 N − 200 N. Answer: 0 N, so the rope's motion does not change.
column29: Opposite directions subtract. What do you get when the two pulls are the same?

column9: On an FBD, the label FN stands for the ___ force.
column28: FN is the normal force: the support force from a surface, always perpendicular (normal) to the surface. On a level floor it points up.
column29: It is the force that keeps objects on top of surfaces.

column9: A **Type A** force problem is one where the object –
column14: is speeding up because the forces are unbalanced
column15: is at rest or moving at a constant velocity
column16: is slowing down because friction is winning
column17: has only one force acting on it
column28: Type A means balanced forces: the object is at rest or moving at constant velocity (Newton's 1st law), so the net force is 0 N. Type B has a net force, so the object accelerates and you use F = ma.
column29: Type A = balanced. What kinds of motion happen when forces are balanced?

column9: Mr. Egg is dropped off the bleachers. If we neglect air resistance, his FBD has only one arrow: Fg pointing down.
column28: True. In free fall with air resistance neglected, gravity is the only force acting on the egg, so the FBD has a single Fg arrow pointing down. There is no normal force because nothing is touching it.
column29: List the forces acting on the egg while it is in the air. Is anything touching it?

column9: A 12 kg box of books sits at rest on a level floor. Use g = 9.8 m/s². What is the normal force (FN) on the box? Answer in N.
column28: At rest on a level surface, FN = Fg. Formula: FN = Fg = m × g. Set up: FN = 12 kg × 9.8 m/s². Answer: 117.6 N up.
column29: The box is at rest, so FN balances the weight. Find the weight with W = m × g.

column9: Jacob drags a sled across the snow with an 85 N pull to the right. Friction on the sled is 23 N to the left. The net force is ___ N to the right. What number goes in the blank? Answer in N.
column28: Opposite directions subtract. Formula: Fnet = Fapp − Ff. Set up: Fnet = 85 N − 23 N. Answer: 62 N to the right, so the sled speeds up to the right.
column29: Fapp and Ff point opposite ways. Subtract the smaller one from the larger one.

column9: A crane cable lifts a crate with a tension of 540 N upward. The crate's weight is 490 N. The net force on the crate is ___ N upward. What number goes in the blank? Answer in N.
column28: Vertical forces in opposite directions subtract. Formula: Fnet = T − Fg. Set up: Fnet = 540 N − 490 N. Answer: 50 N upward, so the crate speeds up going up.
column29: Tension points up and weight points down. Subtract.

column9: Two students push on the same desk. Saffron pushes left with 45 N and Wyatt pushes right with 60 N. What is the net force on the desk?
column15: 105 N to the right
column16: 15 N to the right
column17: 105 N to the left
column28: Opposite directions subtract, and the net force points toward the bigger push. Set up: 60 N − 45 N = 15 N, toward Wyatt's push (right). Adding to get 105 N is the common mistake.
column29: Subtract, then ask: which push is bigger? The net force points that way.

column9: Which of these are **Type A** (balanced forces) situations? Select all that apply.
column14: An orange sitting on a table
column15: A car driving at a steady 55 mph on Hwy 29
column16: An egg dropped from the roof
column17: A skydiver falling at a constant velocity
column18: A car coasting to a stop
column19: A sled speeding up as it is dragged across the snow
column28: Type A means at rest or constant velocity: the orange at rest, the car at a steady 55 mph, and the skydiver at constant velocity. The falling egg is speeding up, the coasting car is slowing down, and the sled is accelerating, so those have a net force (Type B).
column29: Look for objects that are at rest or moving at a steady speed in a straight line.

column9: Put the steps for finding the net force on an object in the correct order.
column14: Sort the forces into horizontal and vertical
column15: Give the direction of the larger side as the net force direction
column16: Draw the FBD and label each force and its direction
column17: Subtract the totals that point in opposite directions
column18: Add the forces that point in the same direction
column28: First list the forces with their directions (draw the FBD), then sort them into horizontal and vertical, then add the forces that point the same way, then subtract the opposite directions, and finally give the direction of the larger side.
column29: You cannot add or subtract until you know which forces line up with each other.

column9: An FBD for a box shows: Fapp = 50 N to the right, Ff = 50 N to the left, Fg = 200 N down, FN = 200 N up. Which is the correct description of the box?
column15: Accelerating to the left
column16: Slowing down while moving right
column17: At rest or moving at constant velocity
column28: Every force has an equal and opposite partner, so the net force is 0 N (Type A). The box is either at rest or moving at constant velocity. Forces being equal does not mean it is slowing down.
column29: Find the net force in each direction. What happens to motion when the net force is zero?

column9: Mrs. Thorpe's car is coasting to the right with her foot off the gas, slowing down. Which FBD description matches?
column14: Ff to the left with no forward force; Fg and FN equal
column15: Fapp to the right longer than Ff to the left; Fg and FN equal
column16: Fapp to the right equal to Ff to the left; Fg and FN equal
column17: Fapp to the right only; Fg longer than FN
column28: Coasting means no forward applied force. Friction (and air resistance) point left, opposite the motion, so the net force is backward and the car slows. Vertically, Fg and FN are equal.
column29: If she is not pressing the gas, is there a forward force? Which way does friction point?

column9: Maya pushes a box right with 40 N, Jae pushes it right with 25 N, and Storm pushes it left with 52 N. The net force is ___ N to the right. What number goes in the blank? Answer in N.
column28: Add the same direction first, then subtract. Set up: right = 40 N + 25 N = 65 N; Fnet = 65 N − 52 N. Answer: 13 N to the right.
column29: Add all the right-pointing forces first, then subtract the left one.

column9: A 2.5 kg textbook rests on a level lab table. Use g = 9.8 m/s². How large is the normal force the table exerts on the book? Answer in N.
column28: At rest on a level surface, FN = Fg. Formula: FN = m × g. Set up: FN = 2.5 kg × 9.8 m/s². Answer: 24.5 N up. Dividing (2.5 ÷ 9.8) is the common mistake.
column29: FN equals the book's weight. Weight = m × g.

column9: Match each FBD description to the motion it shows.
column14: Cart rolling right; Fapp arrow longer than Ff :: Speeding up
column15: Cart rolling right; Fapp arrow same length as Ff :: Constant velocity
column16: Cart rolling right; Ff arrow only, no Fapp :: Slowing down
column17: Book sitting on a table; Fg and FN same length :: At rest
column28: Fapp longer than Ff → net force forward → speeding up. Fapp equal to Ff → balanced → constant velocity. Friction with no forward push → net force backward → slowing down. A book on a table with Fg equal to FN and nothing else → at rest.
column29: Compare the forward arrow to the backward arrow. Which one is longer, or are they equal?

column9: A car driving at a constant 55 mph on Hwy 29 needs a forward force arrow that is longer than its friction and air resistance arrows.
column28: False. Constant velocity means balanced forces (Type A): the forward arrow is the same length as friction plus air resistance. A longer forward arrow would make the car speed up.
column29: Is the car's motion changing? What does that say about the net force?

column9: Addy is a 75 kg skydiver falling at a constant velocity. Use g = 9.8 m/s². How large is the air resistance (Fair) on her? Answer in N.
column28: Constant velocity means balanced forces, so Fair = Fg. Formula: Fair = Fg = m × g. Set up: Fair = 75 kg × 9.8 m/s². Answer: 735 N up.
column29: Constant velocity = Type A. Air resistance must balance her weight.

column9: A football has just been punted and is still rising. Neglecting air resistance, which forces act on the ball?
column14: Fapp from the kick up and Fg down
column15: Fg down only
column16: Fapp from the kick up only
column17: No forces, because the ball is in the air
column28: Once the ball leaves the foot, the kick is no longer pushing it. The only force is gravity (Fg) pointing down, which is why the ball slows as it rises. A force "carried" from the kick is the common misconception.
column29: Is the foot still touching the ball once it is in the air?

column9: A 180 N sign hangs at rest from two vertical ropes that share the weight equally. What is the tension in each rope? Answer in N.
column28: At rest, the upward forces balance the weight: T + T = 180 N. Set up: T = 180 N ÷ 2. Answer: 90 N in each rope.
column29: The two ropes together must hold up the whole sign.

column9: A sled being dragged so it speeds up across the snow has a net force on it, so it is a Type ___ problem.
column28: Speeding up means unbalanced forces and a net force, so it is Type B and you would use F = ma. Type A is balanced (at rest or constant velocity).
column29: Type A is balanced. Is the sled's motion changing?

column9: A model rocket's engine pushes up with 1,500 N. The rocket's weight is 1,200 N. The net force on the rocket is ___ N upward. What number goes in the blank? Answer in N.
column28: Up and down are opposite, so subtract. Formula: Fnet = Fapp − Fg. Set up: Fnet = 1,500 N − 1,200 N. Answer: 300 N upward.
column29: One force points up and one points down. Subtract.

column9: Addy pushes a cart to the right. First she keeps it at a constant speed, then she makes it speed up. Friction stays the same. How does her Fapp arrow compare?
column15: Both Fapp arrows are the same length
column16: The speeding-up Fapp is longer
column17: There is no Fapp while speeding up
column28: At constant speed, Fapp equals Ff. To speed up she needs a net force forward, so the speeding-up Fapp arrow must be longer than the constant-speed one. Thinking constant speed needs a bigger forward arrow is the common mistake.
column29: Speeding up needs a net force. Which push leaves something left over after friction?

column9: Jacob pushes a book to the right across a table and it speeds up. Which forces belong on the book's FBD? Select all that apply.
column15: T pointing up
column16: FN pointing up
column17: Fapp pointing right
column28: The book has Fg (down), FN (up from the table), Fapp (right, Jacob's push), and Ff (left, friction opposing the motion). There is no tension because no rope is attached, and "force of motion" is not a real force.
column29: Go through the labels: gravity, normal, applied, friction, air, tension. Which ones actually act on the book?

column9: Wyatt pushes a dresser right with 75 N and Jacob pushes it right with 58 N. The dresser slides across the carpet at a constant speed. How large is the friction force on the dresser? Answer in N.
column28: Constant speed means balanced forces, so Ff equals the total push. Set up: Ff = 75 N + 58 N. Answer: 133 N to the left.
column29: Constant speed = Type A. Friction must balance both pushes combined.

column9: Storm drags a sled to the right with a 120 N pull. The net force on the sled is 35 N to the right. How large is the friction force on the sled? Answer in N.
column28: Fnet = Fapp − Ff, so Ff = Fapp − Fnet. Set up: Ff = 120 N − 35 N. Answer: 85 N to the left.
column29: Write Fnet = Fapp − Ff, then solve for the missing friction.

column9: A box has these forces: 64 N right, 22 N left, 15 N left, Fg = 300 N down, and FN = 300 N up. The net force is ___ N to the right. What number goes in the blank? Answer in N.
column28: Treat vertical and horizontal separately. Vertical: 300 N − 300 N = 0. Horizontal: left = 22 N + 15 N = 37 N; Fnet = 64 N − 37 N. Answer: 27 N to the right.
column29: Check up/down first (do they cancel?), then add the left forces and subtract from the right one.

column9: A 6.2 kg box sits on top of a 14.5 kg crate, and the stack is at rest on a level floor. Use g = 9.8 m/s². How large is the normal force the floor exerts on the crate? Answer in N.
column28: The floor holds up the whole stack, so FN = total weight. Formula: FN = m × g. Set up: FN = (6.2 kg + 14.5 kg) × 9.8 m/s² = 20.7 kg × 9.8 m/s². Answer: 202.86 N up. Using only the crate's mass is the common mistake.
column29: The floor supports everything sitting on it. Add the masses first.

column9: Tug-of-war: Three students on the left team pull with 210 N, 185 N, and 240 N. Two students on the right team pull with 300 N and 320 N. The net force on the rope is ___ N toward the left team. What number goes in the blank? Answer in N.
column28: Add each team, then subtract. Left = 210 + 185 + 240 = 635 N; right = 300 + 320 = 620 N. Set up: Fnet = 635 N − 620 N. Answer: 15 N toward the left team.
column29: Add each team's pulls first, then subtract the two totals.

column9: A car is moving to the right. Its FBD shows Fapp = 2,400 N to the right, Ff = 650 N to the left, and Fair = 1,900 N to the left (Fg and FN are equal). Which description is correct?
column14: Speeding up to the right; net force 150 N right
column15: Constant velocity; net force 0 N
column16: Slowing down; net force 150 N left
column17: Speeding up to the left; net force 4,950 N left
column28: Left forces: 650 N + 1,900 N = 2,550 N. Net = 2,550 N − 2,400 N = 150 N to the left, opposite the motion, so the car is slowing down while still moving right (Type B).
column29: Add the two left forces, compare to the right force, then ask how a backward net force changes a car moving right.

column9: Jae is a 62 kg skydiver who just jumped. Air resistance on him is 410 N upward. Use g = 9.8 m/s². The net force on Jae is ___ N downward. What number goes in the blank? Answer in N.
column28: Step 1: Fg = m × g = 62 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 607.6 N down. Step 2: Fnet = Fg − Fair = 607.6 N − 410 N. Answer: 197.6 N downward, so he is still speeding up.
column29: Find his weight first, then subtract the air resistance.

column9: A 15 kg sign hangs at rest from two vertical ropes. The left rope pulls up with 80 N. Use g = 9.8 m/s². What is the tension in the right rope? Answer in N.
column28: At rest, T1 + T2 = Fg. Step 1: Fg = 15 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 147 N. Step 2: T2 = 147 N − 80 N. Answer: 67 N up.
column29: Find the sign's weight first. The two ropes together must equal it.

column9: A book rests on a table with Fg = 20 N down and FN = 20 N up. Wyatt says the net force is 40 N. Saffron says it is 0 N. Who is right, and why?
column15: Wyatt, because you add all the forces on an FBD
column16: Wyatt, because the book is pressing on the table
column17: Neither, because the net force is 20 N
column28: Saffron is right. The forces point in opposite directions, so they subtract: 20 N − 20 N = 0 N. Wyatt added forces that point opposite ways. A net force of 0 N matches a book at rest (Type A).
column29: Do forces in opposite directions add or subtract?

column9: Friction on a dresser is 95 N to the left. Saffron pushes it right with 60 N. How hard must Wyatt also push to the right so the dresser slides at a constant speed? Answer in N.
column28: Constant speed means the pushes must add up to friction: 60 N + Fwyatt = 95 N. Set up: Fwyatt = 95 N − 60 N. Answer: 35 N to the right.
column29: Constant speed = balanced. The two pushes together must equal friction.

column9: An FBD shows Fg = 500 N down, FN = 500 N up, Fapp = 80 N right, and Ff = 80 N left. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
column15: The object could be moving at a constant velocity
column16: The object is accelerating to the right
column17: This is a Type A problem
column18: The vertical net force is 1,000 N
column28: Both pairs cancel, so the net force is 0 N, which is Type A: the object is at rest or moving at constant velocity. It is not accelerating, and the vertical forces subtract to 0 N, not add to 1,000 N.
column29: Find the net force in each direction separately. What does a net force of zero tell you?

column9: Addy pulls an 18 kg wagon to the right across level ground with 45 N while friction pulls left with 30 N. Use g = 9.8 m/s². What is the normal force on the wagon? Answer in N.
column28: Treat vertical and horizontal separately. The wagon does not move up or down, so FN = Fg. Set up: FN = 18 kg × 9.8 m/s². Answer: 176.4 N up. The 45 N and 30 N are horizontal and do not change FN.
column29: Normal force is a vertical force. Which numbers in the problem are vertical?

column9: Put the boxes in order from the **smallest** net force to the **largest** net force.
column14: Box C: 15 N right and 25 N right
column15: Box A: 30 N right and 30 N left
column16: Box B: 50 N right and 20 N left
column17: Box D: 70 N left and 60 N right
column28: Box A: 30 − 30 = 0 N. Box D: 70 − 60 = 10 N. Box B: 50 − 20 = 30 N. Box C: 15 + 25 = 40 N (same direction, so add). Order: A, D, B, C.
column29: Find each net force first: same direction add, opposite directions subtract.

column9: A bucket hangs at rest from a rope. The tension in the rope is 63.7 N. Use g = 9.8 m/s². What is the mass of the bucket? Answer in kg.
column28: At rest, T = Fg = m × g, so m = Fg ÷ g. Set up: m = 63.7 N ÷ 9.8 m/s². Answer: 6.5 kg. Multiplying by 9.8 is the common mistake.
column29: The bucket is at rest, so tension equals its weight. Then use m = W/g.

column9: Mr. Egg is falling. On his FBD, the Fg arrow points down and is twice as long as the Fair arrow pointing up. Which is the correct description?
column15: Slowing down as he falls
column16: Moving upward
column17: Speeding up as he falls
column28: Fg is longer than Fair, so the net force points down, the same way he is moving. He is speeding up as he falls (Type B). Equal arrows would mean constant velocity.
column29: Which arrow is longer, and does the net force point with the motion or against it?

column9: If the net force on a sled sliding across the ice is exactly 0 N, the sled will gradually slow down and stop.
column28: False. A net force of 0 N means balanced forces (Type A), so the motion does not change: the sled keeps moving at a constant velocity. Slowing down requires a net force backward, like friction with no forward push.
column29: Does a net force of zero change motion? What would be needed to slow it down?
